subject: Accounting
title: Target Costing
description: A short lesson to help you apply Target Costing.

hook.text: Toyota doesn't set a price after calculating cost. It sets a target cost from the market price.

buildup.text: Target costing starts with what customers will pay and subtracts the desired profit margin.

discovery.text: The result is a maximum allowable cost. Engineers must design the product to hit that number.

twist.text: This reverses traditional thinking—the market sets the cost limit, not the accounting department.

climax.text: Japanese manufacturers pioneered this approach and it's now used across industries worldwide.

punchline.text: Start with the price. Work backward to the cost.

quiz.question: How is a target cost determined?

details.summary: Target costing starts with the market selling price, subtracts the desired profit margin, and works backward to determine the maximum allowable cost for a product. This topic covers the target costing process, value engineering, and its origins in Japanese manufacturing.
details.whyItMatters: Traditional cost-plus pricing starts with cost and adds a margin. Target costing starts with what customers will pay—ensuring products are designed to be profitable from day one rather than needing cost cuts later.
takeaways: Target cost equals the competitive market price minus the required profit margin
Cost reduction happens during the design phase when 80-90% of costs are determined
Value engineering analyzes every component to reduce cost without sacrificing customer value

faq.question: What is target costing?
faq.answer: Target costing is a cost management approach that starts with the competitive selling price, subtracts the desired profit margin, and sets the result as the maximum cost to produce the product. The design team then engineers the product to meet this target cost.

faq.question: How is target costing different from cost-plus pricing?
faq.answer: Cost-plus pricing adds a markup to whatever the product costs to make. Target costing works in reverse: the market determines the price, and the company must design a product that can be made profitably at that price. It forces cost management into the design process.
